title: Learn by Doing: The Language, the Toolchain and Objects
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then the method taught from nothing, with every listing compiled and run.
intro:
Part A is every objective question the bank holds on this topic, the manual's own first.

Part B is empty, and honestly so. Neither past paper sets a written question on the toolchain by itself. It is asked in the objective half, and the skeleton below is the first six lines of every program you will write tomorrow, so the method still earns its place.

lockin.big: "javac turns .java into .class bytecode. java runs the bytecode on the JVM. The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM."
lockin.sub: public static void main(String[] args) is the entry point, and the file name must match the public class name exactly, capital letters included.

methodFrames.teach:
Every Java program starts from the same six lines, and the exam expects you to write them without thinking. Here is the whole skeleton, compiled and run.

public class Hello {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Hello from the JVM");    }}
OutputHello from the JVM
methodFrames.ask: Before the explanation: which word makes this class visible to the JVM, and which line is the entry point?

methodFrames.teach: public makes it visible, and main is the entry point. Word by word: public visible everywhere, static callable without creating an object, void returns nothing, main the name the JVM looks for, String[] args the command line arguments.
methodFrames.ask: The file must be called Hello.java. What happens if you save it as hello.java?

methodFrames.check: It will not compile: the public class name and the file name must match.
methodFrames.teach: javac refuses it: the file name must match the public class name exactly, capital letter included. That is one of the planted errors in a debug question, so look at the class name first.
methodFrames.ask: Two commands build and run it. What does each one produce?

methodFrames.check: javac makes a .class file of bytecode; java runs it on the JVM.
methodFrames.teach: javac Hello.java compiles the source into Hello.class, which holds bytecode, not machine code. java Hello then runs that bytecode on the JVM. Note the second command takes the CLASS name, with no .class on the end.
methodFrames.ask: So why is Java called platform independent, and what is the phrase the examiner wants?

methodFrames.check: Because the bytecode runs on any JVM, so write once, run anywhere.
methodFrames.teach: Write once, run anywhere. The bytecode is the same on every machine, and each platform has its own JVM to run it. That is the whole answer to "why is Java portable".
methodFrames.ask: Last piece of vocabulary: JDK, JRE and JVM. Which contains which?

methodFrames.teach:
The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM. The JDK is for developers and holds javac and the tools; the JRE is what a user needs to run a program; the JVM is the engine inside it. Draw it as three boxes inside one another and the mark is unmissable.

One more pair the objective half asks: a class is the blueprint and an object is one thing built from it. new is what builds it.
